description: Arithmetic, relational and logical operators in Python, plus string slicing and case conversion.
content_html:
Operators — The Tools of Calculation

An operator tells Python how to combine or compare values. There are three categories you must know: arithmetic, relational, and logical. Understanding them precisely matters because exam questions often test the output of specific expressions — especially for relational operators where the expected output is True or False, not “yes” or “no”.

Arithmetic Operators

Python supports six arithmetic operators. Four are familiar: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (real division — the result can be a decimal). The other two are integer division (//) and modulus (%), plus exponentiation (**).

print(17 // 5)    # Integer division: 3 (5 goes into 17 three full times)
print(17 % 5)     # Modulus: 2 (17 = 3*5 + 2, remainder is 2)
print(2 ** 8)     # Exponentiation: 256 (2 to the power of 8)
print(7 / 2)      # Real division: 3.5
Key Fact

The modulus operator (%) returns the remainder after integer division. A classic use is testing whether a number is odd or even: n % 2 == 0 is True if n is even. It also appears in creating circular patterns, validating credit card numbers, and extracting individual digits.

Relational Operators

Relational operators compare two values and always return a Boolean: True or False. This is a common exam error — students write “yes” or “1” when the correct answer is True.

print(10 == 10)   # True
print(10 != 5)    # True
print(3 < 2)      # False
print(5 >= 5)     # True

The six relational operators are: == (equal to), != (not equal to), < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal to), >= (greater than or equal to). Note that == tests equality; a single = in Python is assignment, not comparison.

This is one of the most common errors in exam answers. If a question asks “what is the output of print(7 > 3)?”, the answer is True (capital T, no quotes). Writing “yes” or “1” is wrong. The result of any comparison in Python is a Boolean value — either True or False.

Logical Operators

Logical operators combine or invert Boolean conditions. Python uses and, or, and not (all lowercase).

age = 17
has_consent = True

if age >= 16 and has_consent:
    print("Eligible for trip")

if age < 13 or age > 65:
    print("Reduced price ticket")

if not has_consent:
    print("Permission required")
Key Fact

and requires all combined conditions to be True. or requires at least one to be True. not inverts: not True gives False. These match the Boolean logic used in search queries, access controls, and input validation throughout real systems.

String Operations

Python has powerful built-in tools for working with strings. The length of a string is found with len(). Indexing retrieves a single character by position, starting at 0. Slicing extracts a section of the string.

name = "Computer"
print(len(name))       # 8
print(name[0])         # "C" (first character, index 0)
print(name[3])         # "p" (index 3)
print(name[0:4])       # "Comp" (index 0 up to but not including 4)

For the string s = "GCSE2026":

  • len(s) → 8
  • s[0] → 'G' (first character)
  • s[-1] → '6' (last character, using negative indexing)
  • s[4:8] → '2026' (characters at positions 4, 5, 6, 7)
  • s[0:4] → 'GCSE' (positions 0, 1, 2, 3)

Remember: Python counts from 0, and the end index in a slice is excluded. So s[0:4] gives characters at positions 0, 1, 2, 3 — not position 4.

Case Conversion and Concatenation

Python provides two methods for changing a string’s case: .upper() returns a version with all letters capitalised; .lower() returns a version with all letters in lowercase. These are useful when comparing user input regardless of how it was typed.

city = "London"
print(city.upper())    # "LONDON"
print(city.lower())    # "london"

# Safe comparison:
response = input("Enter yes or no: ")
if response.lower() == "yes":
    print("Confirmed")

Concatenation joins strings together using +. Only strings can be concatenated — trying to add a string and an integer gives a TypeError. Use str() to convert a number to a string first: "Score: " + str(85).

A school system creates a username from the first letter of a student’s first name plus their full surname, all in lowercase:

first_name = input("First name: ")
surname = input("Surname: ")
username = first_name[0].lower() + surname.lower()
print("Username:", username)

If the student enters “Priya” and “Sharma”, the username becomes “psharma”. This uses indexing ([0]), case conversion (.lower()), and concatenation (+) in a single line.
exam_tip_html: For “Identify” or “Give” questions about relational operator output, always write True or False — not “yes”, “1” or “correct”. For string questions, remember Python counts from index 0 and the end index in a slice is excluded. If asked to explain the difference between / and //, give a numeric example: 7 / 2 = 3.5 but 7 // 2 = 3.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Python arithmetic operators include +, -, *, / (real), // (integer), % (modulus) and ** (power). Relational operators always return True or False, not yes or no.
  • Logical operators and, or, and not combine Boolean conditions. and requires all to be True; or requires at least one.
  • String operations: len() for length, s[i] for a character at index i (0-based), s[a:b] for a slice (b excluded), .upper()/.lower() for case, + for concatenation.

practice_questions.text: State the output of the following Python expression: print(17 % 5)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 2 (1). 17 = 3 x 5 + 2; the remainder is 2.
Secure: Correct.
Developing: 3 (confuses modulus with integer division).
Emerging: 3.4 or another incorrect value.

practice_questions.text:
Identify the output of the following Python code:
word = "Science"
print(word[0:3])
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sci (1). Characters at indices 0, 1, 2 — index 3 is excluded.
Secure: Correct.
Developing: Scie (includes index 3 by mistake).
Emerging: sci (incorrect case) or a different portion.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between the / operator and the // operator in Python. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: / performs real (floating-point) division and can return a decimal (1), e.g. 7 / 2 = 3.5 (1); // performs integer division and returns only the whole-number quotient (1), e.g. 7 // 2 = 3 (1).
Secure: Both operators described correctly with one example.
Developing: One operator explained correctly.
Emerging: Confuses the two or provides no examples.

practice_questions.text: Write Python code that takes a full name as input and prints only the first three characters in uppercase.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: input() used and assigned to variable (1); slice [0:3] to extract first three characters (1); .upper() to convert to uppercase (1); print() outputs result (1); meaningful identifier names (1); code runs without error (1).
Secure: Correct logic with minor naming or syntax issue.
Developing: Either slice or upper() present but not both.
Emerging: Attempts but neither slicing nor case conversion used.

practice_questions.text:
State the output of the following Python expression:
print(5 > 3 and 10 < 8)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: False (1). (5 > 3) is True and (10 < 8) is False; True and False = False.
Secure: Correct.
Developing: True (misapplies and logic).
Emerging: Yes or No instead of True or False.

practice_questions.text: A program stores usernames in uppercase. Explain how Python's string methods could be used to ensure a user's input matches a stored username regardless of how they typed it. Write the Python code for the comparison.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains .upper() or .lower() normalises case (1); both the input and stored value should be converted to the same case (1); example: if input_name.upper() == stored_name (1); this means typing 'ali' or 'ALI' or 'Ali' all match the stored value 'ALI' (1).
Secure: Correct idea with working code but partial explanation.
Developing: Mentions .upper() or .lower() without explaining why.
Emerging: No use of case conversion.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the % operator return in Python?
What is the result of 13 // 4 in Python?
What does a relational operator always return in Python?
Name the kind of integer for which n % 2 == 0 returns True in Python.
What Python method converts a string to all lowercase?
For s = 'Computing', what does s[0:4] return?
In Python, what symbol is used for concatenation (joining strings)?
What is the difference between = and == in Python?
flashcard_questions.a: = assigns a value; == tests whether two values are equal.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the and operator require for an expression to evaluate to True?
flashcard_questions.a: All combined conditions must be True.

flashcard_questions.q: What Python operator raises a number to a power?

glossary_terms.definition: A symbol or keyword that tells Python to perform an operation on one or two values, producing a result.
The // operator in Python, which divides two numbers and returns only the whole-number quotient, discarding any remainder.
The % operator in Python, which returns the remainder after integer division.
The ** operator in Python, which raises the left value to the power of the right value.
An operator that compares two values and returns a Boolean result of True or False.
An operator that combines or inverts Boolean conditions: and requires both to be True; or requires at least one to be True; not inverts a Boolean value.
The number of characters in a string, returned by Python's len() function.
Accessing individual characters in a string by their position, starting at index 0 for the first character.
Extracting a portion of a string using Python's slice notation s[start:end], which returns characters from start up to but not including end.
Joining two strings together using the + operator to form a single longer string.
